To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the cis configuration of coding variants is significantly more common than the trans configuration in diploid human exons and that this phenomenon is a key characteristic of human genetic variation.

(1) the cis configuration of coding variants is more abundant than trans in the human genome, (2) the distribution of coding variants in genes is not random but is biased towards the cis configuration, and (3) the distribution of protein-changing variants within genes is also biased, with a subset of genes exhibiting a significant excess of cis configurations of protein-changing variants.
the cis-abundance of variants is a common phenomenon in human genomes, and it is associated with a specific set of genes that are important for human adaptation.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the phase of protein-coding variants in diploid genomes.
the distribution of variants between chromosomes, and how this distribution impacts gene function and phenotype.
the phase of variants in human genomes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the majority of the genes in the human genome have a higher frequency of cis-configurations, but there are also genes that show a higher frequency of trans-configurations.
the cis/trans ratio is not 50:50, but varies between genes and populations, and is significantly skewed towards cis in many cases.
the cis-abundance is the result of the evolutionary pressure for adaptation, and that it is not a result of the genetic drift.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have shown that cis-configuration of protein-altering variants are more abundant than trans-configurations.
the distribution of protein-changing variants between two copies of the gene in a genome is highly non-random.
cis-configurations of variants are more common than trans-configurations in diploid human exons and this is likely to be functionally important.
The main takeaway from our work is that
cis-configurations of genetic variants are more common than trans-configurations, and that this pattern holds across all human populations.

cis-abundant genes are more frequent than trans-abundant genes in the human population and are enriched in genes with important functions for adaptation and evolution, and thus are of particular interest to researchers.
cis-configurations of genetic variants are significantly overrepresented in diploid human exons, and that the functional consequences of this phenomenon are far reaching.
